notes.b: A fibre is a hair-like strand, the raw material that is spun into yarn and then made into fabric. Fibres are grouped by where their raw material comes from and how the fibre is formed, which gives three classes: natural, regenerated and synthetic.
points: Staple fibres are short, such as cotton, wool and linen, so they must be twisted together to make a yarn. Filaments are continuous and very long, such as silk and all man-made fibres as they are extruded (pushed out).
Natural fibres are obtained directly from plants or animals and need only cleaning and processing before they are spun into yarn, which is why they are the simplest class.

Natural fibres of plant origin are made of cellulose (the plant material that forms cell walls), and are called cellulosic: cotton, linen, and also hemp and jute. Natural fibres of animal origin are made of protein: wool and silk.

Regenerated fibres are made by dissolving a natural polymer (a long chain molecule), usually cellulose from wood pulp, and forcing the solution through a spinneret (a plate with fine holes) so that it reforms as a fibre. Examples are viscose (rayon), acetate and triacetate.

Synthetic fibres are made entirely from chemicals: small molecules called monomers, derived from coal or petroleum, are built into polymers. Examples are nylon (polyamide), polyester, acrylic and elastane (Lycra).
Regenerated and synthetic fibres together are called man-made (manufactured) fibres.
Diagram: a classification tree branching from textile fibres into natural (plant and animal), regenerated and synthetic, with one named example at the end of each branch.
notes.tip: A larger fabric-profile question often starts by asking you to name the fibre class, so state natural, regenerated or synthetic first. Regenerated is man-made but is not natural, and silk is a natural protein fibre, never synthetic.

notes.b: Each natural fibre comes from one plant or animal source, and that source decides what the fibre is made of and what it is used for. Learn one source, one use and one property for each of the four main fibres.
points: Cotton: a cellulose fibre from the seed hairs of the cotton plant (the boll); used for shirts, jeans, T-shirts, towels, bed linen and curtains. It is absorbent and cool to wear.
Linen: a cellulose fibre from the stem of the flax plant; used for tea towels, tablecloths, summer clothing and bed linen. It is strong and absorbent, so it suits cloths that must dry dishes.
Wool: a protein fibre from the fleece of sheep; used for jumpers, knitwear, tweed, suits, blankets and carpets. It is warm and resilient (springs back into shape).

Silk: a protein filament from the cocoon of the silkworm (the caterpillar of the silk moth, fed on mulberry leaves); used for scarves, ties, formal and evening wear, lingerie and luxury bedding. It is smooth, drapes well and is absorbent.
Cotton and linen absorb moisture readily and are cool to wear; wool and silk are warm because they trap air in their structure.

Natural fibres are popular for household textiles because they are absorbent, comfortable, durable, washable, and accept dyes and finishes well. They come from renewable sources, and many people simply prefer natural fabric.
notes.tip: When asked to classify natural fibres, give plant (cotton, linen) and animal (wool, silk) with an example and a use of each. If asked for properties of one named fibre, give three, and remember wool and silk are protein, not cellulose.

notes.b: Regenerated fibres start from cellulose that already exists in a plant. The cellulose is dissolved and re-formed as a long filament, which is why they are called regenerated.
points: Viscose (rayon): cellulose from wood pulp is treated with chemicals, dissolved and forced through a spinneret into a chemical bath, where the fibre reforms. Rayon and viscose are the same fibre family, not two different fibres.
Viscose is absorbent, soft, drapes well and dyes well, but it is weak when wet, so it needs gentle handling. It is used for dresses, blouses, linings and soft furnishings.
Acetate: cellulose is chemically combined with acetic acid, dissolved and extruded to form a fibre with a silky, lustrous appearance. Triacetate is a related fibre.
Acetate drapes well, so it is used for linings, blouses and evening wear. It is also used for ties.
Lyocell is a newer regenerated cellulose fibre made by dissolving wood pulp in a solvent; it is absorbent and soft, much like other cellulose fibres such as cotton.
Regenerated fibres start from a plant-based raw material, wood pulp cellulose, so they are classed apart from synthetics, which start from coal or petroleum chemicals.
notes.tip: Say only that the raw material of regenerated fibres is plant cellulose. Do not claim they are made without chemicals, because making viscose uses strong chemicals. Acetate and triacetate are called regenerated in marking schemes, so follow that.

notes.b: Synthetic fibres are built from chemicals rather than grown, so their properties can be designed. Each one has a typical strength that decides where it is used.
points: Nylon (polyamide): made from chemicals derived from coal or petroleum; very strong, elastic, light, abrasion resistant and low in absorbency. Used for hosiery, swimwear, jackets, carpets and ropes.
Polyester: made from petroleum-based chemicals; strong, crease resistant and quick drying. Used for shirts, fleece, curtains and bed linen, and often blended with cotton.
Acrylic: made from a polymer of acrylonitrile; it resembles wool, being soft, warm and light, so it is used for knitwear, socks and blankets.
Elastane is a stretch fibre; Lycra is a brand name for it. It is usually blended in small amounts with other fibres, for swimwear, sportswear and hosiery.
Synthetic fibres can be produced in a range of thicknesses and lustres by changing the spinneret holes and the amount of drawing.
notes.tip: Lycra is a brand of elastane, so note this if you use the name as a generic term, although the examination accepts Lycra as an answer. Name the fibre together with a property or use to get the mark.

notes.b: Both are man-made and both are extruded through a spinneret, but they begin with different raw materials and behave differently. Compare them point by point: source, process, moisture, heat and an example.
points: Source: regenerated fibres begin with a natural polymer, cellulose from wood pulp; synthetic fibres begin with small molecules, called monomers, made from coal or petroleum.
Process: regenerated fibres are dissolved and reformed from an existing natural polymer; synthetic fibres are formed by linking monomers into a polymer, then extruding it.
Moisture: regenerated fibres such as viscose absorb moisture like cotton and drape well; synthetic fibres such as polyester absorb little moisture, so they dry quickly and resist creasing.
Heat: nylon and polyester melt at high temperatures, because they are plastic-like polymers, whereas viscose chars and burns like cotton.
For example, regenerated fibres include viscose and acetate; synthetic fibres include nylon, polyester and acrylic.
Example in use: a viscose blouse is more absorbent and comfortable next to the skin; a polyester blouse resists creasing and dries more quickly.
notes.tip: Differentiate questions ask for raw material, how each is made, and an example of each, so cover all three. Say regenerated starts from a natural polymer (cellulose), while synthetic is built from chemicals from coal or petroleum.

notes.b: Regenerated and synthetic fibres are made in the same basic way: a thick liquid is pushed through tiny holes and hardened into long filaments. The steps below apply to both.
points: 1. A thick liquid, either a molten polymer or a polymer solution, is forced through a spinneret, a metal plate with many fine holes.
2. The emerging streams harden: by cooling in air (melt spinning), by setting in a chemical bath (wet spinning), or by warm air evaporating the solvent (dry spinning).
3. The filaments are drawn, or stretched, so that their molecules line up, which makes them stronger.
Diagram: a spinneret cross-section showing polymer pumped through holes, forming filaments that are drawn onto a winding bobbin.

keyTerms.definition: A fibre obtained directly from a plant or animal, which needs only cleaning and processing before it is spun into yarn.
A man-made fibre formed by dissolving a natural polymer, usually cellulose, and reforming it as a fibre.
A man-made fibre formed from polymers made from chemicals derived from coal or petroleum.
A natural polymer found in plant cell walls, the main component of cotton, linen and wood pulp.
A natural fibre made of protein, such as wool (keratin) or silk (fibroin).
A long chain of repeated small molecular units that forms the basis of all fibres.
A small molecule that links with others to form a polymer.
A metal plate with many fine holes through which a polymer is forced to form filaments.

Cellulose from wood pulp, dissolved in chemicals and reformed as a fibre.

questions.prompt: Name one natural fibre of plant origin, one protein fibre and one synthetic fibre. State one use of each.
questions.model: Cotton (plant origin): used for towels or shirts. Wool or silk (protein): wool is used for knitwear or blankets; silk is used for scarves or ties. Nylon, polyester or acrylic (synthetic): nylon for hosiery or carpets; polyester for shirts or curtains; acrylic for knitwear or socks.

questions.prompt: Compare regenerated fibres with synthetic fibres. Refer to their raw materials, how each is made and one property of each, and give one example of each type.
questions.model: Raw materials: regenerated fibres such as viscose and acetate start from cellulose, usually from wood pulp; synthetic fibres such as nylon and polyester start from chemicals derived from coal or petroleum. Manufacture: cellulose is dissolved in chemicals and forced through a spinneret to reform as a fibre; synthetic polymers are formed by linking monomers, then extruded through a spinneret and drawn. Properties: viscose is absorbent and drapes well, and it chars and burns like cotton; polyester absorbs little moisture, dries quickly, resists creasing and melts at high temperatures. Examples: viscose for dresses or linings; polyester for shirts, fleece or curtains.
